la:other:Philippus.html:
Phĭlippus, i, m., = Φίλιππος,
Philip, the name of several kings of Macedonia, the most celebrated of whom was the son of Amyntas, and father of Alexander the Great, ; ; ; ; cf. .—
Transf., a gold coin struck by KingPhilip, a Philippe d'or, ; so ; 41; 78 al.; ; and, in gen., of other coins,.—
Hence,
Phĭlippēus (collat. form Phĭlippĭus, ), a, um, adj., = Φιλίππειος, of or belonging to Philip, king of Macedonia, Philippian: Philippeus sanguis,i. e. Cleopatra, because the Egyptian sovereigns were descended from Philip of Macedon, (4, 10, 40): Em tibi talentum argenti: Philippeum aes est,: Philippeus nummus, a gold coin struck by Philip, of the value of twenty drachmœ, a Philippe d'or: nummi Philippei aurei,; : Philippeum aurum,from which the Philippe d'or was struck,— Hence, absol.: Phĭlippēum, i, n., a gold coin struck by Philip, Varr. ap. . —And, transf., of other coins: argenteos Philippeos minutulos, Val. Imp. ap. .—
Phĭlippĭcus, a, um, adj., = Φιλιππικός, of or belonging to Philip, Philippic: Philippicum talentum argenti,: aurum,a gold-mine of Philip's in Macedonia,. —Cicero's orations against Antony were called orationes Philippicae, after those of Demosthenes against King Philip, .—Also sing. collect.: Phĭlippĭca, ae, f.: divina Philippica,.

la:noun:philologus.html:
phĭlŏlŏgus, a, um, adj., = φιλόλογος.
Of or belonging to learning, learned, literary: philologis et philotechnis rebus me delectans, prooem. 4: homines,.—
Esp. of persons.
Scholarly, learned, versed in history, antiquities, and literature (implying a broader culture than grammaticus, litterator; v. Krebs, Antibarb. 863 sq.): homines nobiles illi quidem, sed nullo modo philologi,.—Subst.: phĭlŏlŏgus, i, m. —
In gen., a person engaged in learned or literary pursuits, a man of letters, learned man, scholar (class.): Atteius Philologi appellationem assumpsisse videtur, quia, sicut Eratosthenes, qui primus hoc cognomen sibi vindicavit, multiplici variāque doctrinā censebatur,: cum Ciceronis librum de republicā prendit hinc philologus aliquis, hinc grammaticus, hinc philosophiae deditus, alius alio curam suam mittit; ... hoc subnotat (philologus): duos Romanos reges esse, etc.,.

la:noun:philosophia.html:
phĭlŏsŏphĭa, ae, f., = φιλοσοφία,
philosophy.
Lit.: nec quicquam aliud est philosophia, si interpretari velis, quam studium sapientiae,: omnia quae in philosophiā tractantur,; : ars est enim philosophia vitae,; ; et saep.: videte ne quis vos decipiat per philosophiam,.—
Transf.
A philosophical subject or question: circulus, in quo de philosophiā sermo habetur,.—
In plur.: phĭlŏsŏphĭae, ārum, f., philosophical systems or sects: exercitatio propria duarum philosophiarum (i. e. Academicorum et Peripateticorum),; ; .

la:other:Philippi.html:
Phĭlippi, ōrum, m., = Φίλιπποι,
a city in Macedonia, on the borders of Thrace, celebrated for the battle in which Octavianus and Antony defeated Brutus and Cassius, now Filibi, ; ; ; ; .—Hence,
Phĭ-lippensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Philippi, Philippian: Philippense bellum,: proelium,the battle of Philippi,: Brutus,who fell at Philippi,.—
Phĭlip-pēus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Philippi, Philippian: campi,; .—

la:noun:phaselus.html:
phăsēlus (phăsell- and făs-), i, m. and f., = φάσηλος.
Lit., a kind of bean with an edible pod, French beans, kidney-beans, phasel (phaseolus vulgaris of Linn.): viciamque seres vilemque phaselum,: longa fasellus,; v. ; .—
Transf., a light vessel (in the shape of a kidney-bean) made of wicker-work or papyrus, sometimes also of burned and painted clay (cf.: celox, lembus): epistulam de phaselo dare,: phaselus ille quem videtis,: phaselon solvere,: dare vela fictilibus phaselis,: pictam phaselon,.

la:noun:phalerae.gloss: a metal disc or boss, especially worn as a military ornament on the breast
senses: a metal disc or boss, especially worn as a military ornament on the breast
a trapping for the forehead and breast of horses
la:noun:phalerae.html:
phălĕrae, ārum (
neutr. phalera posita, ; Jan. phaleras), f., = τὰ φάλαρα.
Lit.
A smooth, shining ornament for the breast, a metal disc or boss, worn by men, esp. as a military decoration: phalerae sunt belli ornamenta,; : phaleris et torque aliquem donare : phaleras deponere,; cf. : phaleris hic pectora fulget,.—As a military mark of distinction: equites donati phaleris,; Heyn. and Wagn.; .—Worn by women: matrona ornata phaleris pelagiis, P. Syrus ap. . —
A trapping for the forehead and breast of horses, : primus equum phaleris insignem victor habeto,; ; .—As a trapping for elephants, .—
Trop., an external ornament or decoration (poet. and in post-class. prose): ad populum phaleras! trappings for the people! who allow themselves to be deceived by externals, .—Of rhetorical ornament, : loquendi,: heroicorum,

la:noun:Phaedrus.html:
Phaedrus (nom. PHAEDER, ), i, m., = Φαῖδρος.
A pupil of Socrates, a native of Myrsinus, in Attica, after whom Plato named one of his dialogues, ; ; ; ; —
An Epicurean philosopher of Athens, an instructor of Cicero, ; ; ; .—
A freedman of Augustus, a Thracian by birth, and author of some well-known Latin fables.

la:adj:philosophus.html:
phĭlŏsŏphus, a, um, adj., = φιλόσοφος,
philosophical: philosopha sententia, Pac. ap. : scriptiones,: verbum,: tractatus,, § 13.—
Subst.
phĭ-lŏsŏphus, i, m., a philosopher: philosophi denique ipsius, qui de suā vi ac sapientiā unus omnia paene profitetur, est tamen quaedam descriptio, ut is, qui studeat, omnium rerum divinarum atque humanarum vim, naturam causasque nosse et omnem bene vivendi rationem tenere et persequi, nomine hoc appelletur,: alio tempore rhetorum praecepta tradere, alio philosophorum,: nemo aegrotus quicquam somniat tam infandum, quod non aliquis dicat philosophus, Varr. ap. ; cf. .—Plur.: Stoici philosophi,.—
phĭlŏsŏpha, ae, f., a female philosopher: ea villa tamquam philosopha videtur esse,; so in apposition: philosopha anicula, Verus ap. Vulcat. Av.—Hence, adv.: phĭlŏsŏphē, philosophically: in his ipsis prooemiis philosophe scribere voluimus,.—Ironically, .

phĭlŏsŏphor, ātus, 1,
v. dep. n. [philosophus], to apply one's self to philosophy, to play the philosopher, to philosophize (class.): philosophatur quoque jam, non mendax modo'st,; : philosophari est mihi necesse, at paucis, Enn. ap. (cited periphrastically ap. ; ; ; cf. Trag. Rel. v. 417 Vahl., and p. 53 Rib.); ; : sed jam satis est philosophatum,.

Lit., a quiver for holding arrows (poet. and late Lat.): succinctam pharetrā,: nec venenatis gravida sagittis, Fusce, pharetra,: pharetram solvere,to undo, open,: venatricis puellae (Dianae),: in pharetrā suā abscondit me,; ; ; ; ; ; —
Transf., a kind of sundial in the form of a quiver, .

la:noun:Phoebus.html:
Phoebus, i, m., = Φοῖβος (the radiant),
a poetical appellation of Apollo as the god of light: quae mihi Phoebus Apollo Praedixit,; ; .—Poet. for the sun: dum rediens fugat astra Phoebus,: Phoebi pallidus orbis,; : tristior iccirco nox est, quam tempora Phoebi,.—Hence,
Phoe-bēĭus, a, um, adj., Phœbean, Apollinean: juvenis,i. e. Æsculapius,: anguis,of Æsculapius,: ictus,of the sun,: ales, the raven, so called because metamorphosed by Apollo, : oscen,: Idmon,son of Phœbus,: Circe,daughter of Sol,.—
Phoe-bēus, a, um, adj., Phœbean, Apollinean: carmina,: lampas,the sun,: virgo,Daphne,: laurus,: Rhodos,where the worship of Apollo prevailed,: lyra,: sortes,oracle,: tripodes,: Phoebeā morbos pellere arte,.—
Phoebas, ădis, f., a priestess of Apollo; hence the inspired one, the prophetess, ; ; ; .

The son of Amyntor, who was given by Peleus to Achilles as a companion in the Trojan war, ; ; ; . He brought to Peleus the news of the death of Achilles, .—
A son of Agenor, brother of Cadmus and Europa, .

la:noun:phalanx.html:
phălanx (post-class. fălanx), angis, f., = φάλαγξ.
In gen.
Lit., a band of soldiers, a host drawn up in close order (poet.): Agamemnoniae phalanges,: densae,: Tuscorum,: animosa (said of eight brothers fighting together),: junctae umbone phalanges,.—
Trop., a host, multitude (postclass.): culparum,.—
In partic.
Among the Athenians and Spartans, a division of an army drawn up in battle array, a battalion, phalanx, ; .—
The Macedonian order of battle, a Macedonian phalanx (a compact parallelogram of fifty men abreast and sixteen deep), ; ; ; cf.: quae (cohortes) cuneum Macedonum (phalangem ipsi vocant) perrumperent,: fecerat et falangem triginta milium hominum,.—
An order of battle of the Gauls and Germans, forming a parallelogram: Helvetii confertissimā acie, phalange factā, etc.,; : phalangem perfringere,.

la:other:Phoebe.html:
Phoēbē, ēs, f., = Φοίβη.
The moongoddess, sister of Phœbus, i. e. Diana, Luna, or the moon: vento semper rubet aurea Phoebe,; ; : Phoebe venantibus assit,: jaculatrix Phoebe,: innupta,; .—
Transf., night: tertia,.—
A daughter of Leda and sister of Helen, .—
Daughter of Leucippus, ; .

la:noun:Phaethon.html:
Phăĕthon (dissyl.: fulmine Phaethon, Varr. ap. ), ontis, m., = Φαέθων (the shining one).
Son of Helios and Clymene, who, having obtained from his father permission to drive the sun's chariot for a day, lost control of the steeds, and was struck down by a thunderbolt of Jupiter, to prevent his setting the earth on fire, ; ; cf.: Phaëthontem orbi terrarum educare,; ; .—
An epithet of the sun (poet.), ; .—Hence,
Phăĕ-thontēus, a, um, adj., = Φαεθόντειος, of or belonging to Phaëthon, Phaëthontean (poet.): ignes,: Padus (because Phaëthon is said to have fallen into the Padus),: favilla, i. e. fulmen,: umbra, i. e. of the poplar (because the sisters of Phaëthon were changed into poplars), .—
Phăĕthontĭas, ădis, f., = Φαεθοντιάς, a Phaëthontiad, i. e. a sister of Phaëthon. They wept for their brother, and were changed into poplars (acc. to others, into alders), while their tears were converted into amber: Phaëthontiadum silva sororum,; ; cf. sqq.—
Phăĕthentis, ĭdis, f., = Φαεθοντίς, subst., i. q. Phaëthontias, a Phaëthontiad, a sister of Phaëthon (poet.), .—As adj., of or belonging to Phaëthon, Phaëthontian: gutta, amber (into which the tears of Phaëthon's sisters were said to be converted), .—
Phăĕthontĭus, a, um, adj., = Φαεθόντιος.
Of or belonging to Phaëthon, Phaëthontian: fabula,: amnis, i.e. Padus (v. Phaëthonteus),. —
Of or belonging to the sun: ora,the sun's disk,.

la:other:Phegeus.html:
Phēgeus, i, m., = Φηγεύς,
the father of Alphesibœa, .—Hence,
Phēgēïus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Phegeus, Phegean: Phegeius ensis,.—
Phēgis, ĭdis, f., = Φηγίς, daughter of Phegeus, Alphesibœa; acc. Phegida, .

la:noun:Phlegethon.gloss: a river in the Lower World
senses: a river in the Lower World
la:noun:Phlegethon.html:
Phlĕgĕthon, ontis, m., = Φλεγέθων (burning, blazing),
a river in the Lower World, which ran with fire instead of water: Chaos et Phlegethon loca nocte silentia late,: Tartareus,; : ardenti freto Phlegethon harenas igneus tostas agens,; ; . —Hence,
Phlĕgĕthontēus, a, um, adj., Phlegethontian: ripa,.—
Phlĕgĕthontis, ĭdis, f.adj., Phlegethontian: unda,: lympha,.

la:noun:pharus.html:
Phărus or -os, i, f. (m., ), = Φάρος.
An island near Alexandria, in Egypt, where King Ptolemy Philadelphus built a famous light-house, hence called pharus, now Faro, ; Auct. B. Alex. 19.—
Transf., of the lighthouse in the island of Pharos: Pharus est in insulā turris, magnā altitudine, mirificis operibus exstructa, quae nomen ab insulā accepit,: superposuit turrem in exemplum Alexandrini Phari,; ; of other light-houses: pharon subiit,: turris phari terrae motu Capreis concidit,: Tyrrhena,.—
Transf., poet., Egypt: regina Phari,: petimus Pharon arvaque Lagi,.— Hence,
Phărĭăcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pharus, Pharian, Egyptian (post-class.): sistra,.—
Phărĭus, a, um, adj., = Φάριος, of or belonging to Pharus, Pharian; of the lighthouse: flammae,.—Poet., transf., Egyptian: Pharia juvenca, i. e. Io, ; but Isis, ; nence, turba,the priests of Isis,: conjux,i. e. Cleopatra,: dolores,the lamentations of the Egyptian women at the festival of Isis for the lost Osiris,: piscis,i. e. the crocodile,: acetum,.—As subst.: Phărĭa, ae, f., Isis: SACRVM PHARIAE, Vet. Kalend. ap. Grut. 138.—
Phărītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Pharos, Auct. B. Alex. 19.—
A small island on the coast of Dalmatia, formerly called Paros (Parus), now Lesina, .

la:noun:phantasma.html:
phantasma, ătis, n., = φάντασμα.
An apparition, spectre, phantom (postAug.; cf.: idolon, imago, simulacrum): velim scire, esse phantasmata et habere figuram ... an inania, etc.,: si phantasma fuit Christus,; ; .—
In gen., an image, appearance, phantasm of an object (late Lat. for visum, imago, species): Alexandriam cum eloqui volo, quam nunquam vidi, praesto est apud me phantasma ejus,.

Subst.
phўsĭcus, i, m., a natural philosopher, naturalist: ut ait physicus Anaxagoras,: Democritus,: non pudet igitur physicum, id est speculatorem venatoremque naturae, petere, etc.,; .—Plur., ; .—
phўsĭca, ōrum, n., physics: physicorum ignarus,: in physicis alienus,not versed in,.—Hence, adv.: phўsĭcē, in the manner of naturalists, physically: dicere,.

Pharaoh, the title of the Egyptian kings: Pharao nomen est non hominis, sed honoris, sicut apud nos Augusti appellantur reges, cum propriis nominibus censeantur,; ; et saep.

la:adj:Pharisaeus.html:
Phărĭsaeus, i, m., = Φαρισαῖος,
a Pharisee, a member of the Jewish sect of that name, usually in plur.: Phărĭsaei (Pharīsaei, ), ōrum, m., = Φαρισαῖοι, the Pharisees, a Jewish sect (eccl. Lat.), ; ; ; et saep.— Sing.: secundum legem Pharisaeus,.—Hence,
Phărĭsaeus, a, um, adj., = Φαρισαῖος, Pharisœan: convivia,; .—

la:noun:physicus.html:

phўsĭcus, i, m., a natural philosopher, naturalist: ut ait physicus Anaxagoras,: Democritus,: non pudet igitur physicum, id est speculatorem venatoremque naturae, petere, etc.,; .—Plur., ; .—
phўsĭca, ōrum, n., physics: physicorum ignarus,: in physicis alienus,not versed in,.—Hence, adv.: phўsĭcē, in the manner of naturalists, physically: dicere,.

la:adj:philosophicus.html:

A phantom, apparition: (animus) colli-git visa nocturna, quas phantasias nos adpellamus,.

la:other:Phoenice.html:
Phoenīcē, ēs (Phoenīca, , v. Madv. ad loc.; Poenīcē, al.), f., = Φοινίκη,
Phœnicia, a country of Syria, especially celebrated for the purple which came from there; its principal cities were Tyre and Sidon, ; ; ; ; ; ; .—Called also Phoenīcĭa, ae, f., , §§ 678, 680; ; .—
A small island in the Ægean Sea, otherwise called Ios, .—
A town of Epirus, .—
Vid. phoenicea.— Hence,
Phoenīces, um, m., the Phœnicians, celebrated as the earliest navigators and as founders of many colonies, especially of Carthage, ; ; ; ; .—In sing.: Phoenix, a Phœnician, Cadmus, .—
Transf., the Carthaginians, ; in sing., a Carthaginian, .—Adj., Phœnician: elate,.—
phoenī-cĕus (poenī-, foenī-), a, um, adj., = φοινίκεος, purple-red: aut phoeniceum florem habet aut purpureum, aut lacteum,; cf. : poeniceas vestes,: poeniceum corium,i. e. made purple-red with blows,.—
Phoenīcĭus, a, um, adj., Phœnician: mare,.—
Phoenissus, a, um, adj., Phœnician: Dido,: exsul,i. e. Anna,: Tyros,.—As subst.: Phoenissa, ae, f.: Dido,.—Plur.: Phoenissae, the Phœnician women, the name of a tragedy by Euripides; also of one by Seneca.—
Transf.
Theban, because Cadmus was a Phœnician: cohors,.—
Carthaginian: classis,: juventa,.—In neutr. plur.: Phoenissa agmina,.—Subst.: Phoenissa, ae, f., Carthage, .—
Phoenīcĭas, ae, m., the south-south-east wind, .

la:other:Pharus.html:
Phărus or -os, i, f. (m., ), = Φάρος.
An island near Alexandria, in Egypt, where King Ptolemy Philadelphus built a famous light-house, hence called pharus, now Faro, ; Auct. B. Alex. 19.—
Transf., of the lighthouse in the island of Pharos: Pharus est in insulā turris, magnā altitudine, mirificis operibus exstructa, quae nomen ab insulā accepit,: superposuit turrem in exemplum Alexandrini Phari,; ; of other light-houses: pharon subiit,: turris phari terrae motu Capreis concidit,: Tyrrhena,.—
Transf., poet., Egypt: regina Phari,: petimus Pharon arvaque Lagi,.— Hence,
Phărĭăcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pharus, Pharian, Egyptian (post-class.): sistra,.—
Phărĭus, a, um, adj., = Φάριος, of or belonging to Pharus, Pharian; of the lighthouse: flammae,.—Poet., transf., Egyptian: Pharia juvenca, i. e. Io, ; but Isis, ; nence, turba,the priests of Isis,: conjux,i. e. Cleopatra,: dolores,the lamentations of the Egyptian women at the festival of Isis for the lost Osiris,: piscis,i. e. the crocodile,: acetum,.—As subst.: Phărĭa, ae, f., Isis: SACRVM PHARIAE, Vet. Kalend. ap. Grut. 138.—
Phărītae, ārum, m., the inhabitants of Pharos, Auct. B. Alex. 19.—
A small island on the coast of Dalmatia, formerly called Paros (Parus), now Lesina, .

la:noun:phasis.html:
Phāsis, ĭdis or ĭdos (acc. also Phasin, ; :
Phasim,; voc. Phasĭ, ), m., = Φᾶσις.
A river in Colchis, which empties into the Euxine Sea, now Rion, ; : limosi Phasidos undae,: sua jura cruentum Phasin habent,: Phasidis ales, a pheasant (v. in the foll. Phasiacus), ; cf.: ultra Phasin capi volunt, quod ambitiosam popinam instruat,.—
Transf., a town and its harbor lying at the mouth of the Phasis, a colony of the Milesians, now Poti, ; .—Hence,
Phāsis, ĭdis, adj. f., Phasian;poet.Colchian: volucres,i. e. pheasants,.—Subst.: Phāsis, ĭdis, f., the Colchian, a term applied to Medea; acc. Phasida, .—
Phā-sĭăcus, a, um, adj., = Φασιακός, of or belonging to the Phasis, Phasian; also poet.Colchian: angulus,: unda,: terra,: corona, whichMedea presented to Creusa, : ales Phasiacis petita Colchis,i. e. the pheasant,.—
Phāsĭānus, a, um, adj., = Φασιανός, of or belonging to the Phasis, Phasian: Phasianae aves,pheasants,.—As subst.: phāsĭāna, ae, f., a pheasant, .— More freq., phāsĭānus (fāsĭān-), i, m., ; ; ; Edict. Diocl. p. 14.—According to the myth, it is the metamorphosed Itys, daughter of Tereus; v. Itys.—
Phā-sĭas, ădis, adj. f., = Φασιάς, of or belonging to the Phasis, Phasian;poet.Colchian: Phasias Aeetine,: puella,i. e. Medea,.—Subst.: Phāsĭas. ădis, f., Medea, .
